limits: One repository. Absolute scores are not comparable to any external benchmark; the method-to-method comparison is what this corpus supports.
Author concentration: a corpus dominated by one author inherits that author’s commit-message style, which biases absolute recall for every method equally.
A commit message is a POST-HOC description of a change, not a bug report written before the fix. It is a better proxy for "an agent is told what to change" than for "an agent is told what is broken".
Ground truth is file-level. A method that finds the right file but the wrong symbol inside it scores as a hit.

tasks.question: feat(embed): one-command semantic tier, and the measured model ladder behind it Closes the gap that decided the first five minutes against Mem0: a fresh crib answered paraphrased questions at 2.6%, and the documented fix was three commands whose last step named ` ` — a directory the published package does not contain. ` ` ships ["dist","skills","LICENSE","NOTICE"], so for anyone who installed from npm the instructions could not be followed at all. The tier was git-checkout-only. `crib embed setup` replaces it. One command: it resolves a Python, checks for sentence-transformers, confirms the weights are cached, GENERATES the adapter into the embed home, pins it through the same integrity path a hand-installed model takes, and then proves it ranks before reporting success. Verified end to end, not asserted: crib embed setup --model large → gates, G2 0.8104575163398693 which reproduces the published 81.0% to every digit. The generated adapter also reproduces the hand-written one exactly (G2 0.6601307189542484 for `small`), so the convenience path costs nothing in quality. THE MODEL LADDER ( ) Five models, each run through the frozen launch gate with only the embedder changed. Nothing here is estimated: large multilingual-e5-large 2.1 GB 81.0% PASS base multilingual-e5-base 1.1 GB 69.9% small all-MiniLM-L6-v2 87 MB 66.0% — para-multi-mpnet-base 1.0 GB 59.5% — para-multi-MiniLM-L12 458 MB 47.1% — (no tier) char-ngram 0 B 2.6% Two findings worth the run. First, ONLY `large` clears the 80% threshold, so there is no honest "ship a small model as the semantic tier" option — `large` stays the default and the rest are labelled as not passing. Second, SIZE DOES NOT PREDICT QUALITY: the 87 MB English model beats a 458 MB and a 1.0 GB multilingual one. Reasoning from parameter count would have shipped a worse default at 5-11x the download. `small` still earns a place: 66.0% is 25x the fallback for 4% of the download. A test asserts the table can never claim for a model below the threshold. ALSO - The adapter path sanitiser let `..` survive into a path segment. Not exploitable — separators are replaced, so the result stays under the embed home — but the segment is now defended on its own terms rather than by an argument about its caller. Found by a test written against the invariant. - `crib init` now names the tier in its next steps with both numbers, because a user who stops after `crib memory init` gets 2.6% recall and no signal that a better tier exists. - `crib doctor`'s fix hint and the tier report's install hint both point at the one command instead of the unfollowable repo path. - had no memory matrix at all — it compared only code-graph tools while the positioning claims to replace Mem0. Adds one, with crib's cells measured and every competitor cell explicitly labelled as a capability claim read from their docs, not a benchmark run here. The row crib loses (semantic recall out of the box) is in the table, not a footnote. Verified: 2,613 tests pass, biome clean over 555 files, `pnpm budget:check` ok (the adapter is generated at setup time, so no model or dependency enters the 5 MB package). tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: fix(freshness): elect exactly one worker and fence a superseded owner (R01) `start()` read the lease, checked liveness, then wrote its own state with no lock spanning the decision, so N processes starting together each concluded they owned a single-owner service: twelve trials of eight contenders admitted 5-8 owners. Because every claimant then overwrote the same `activeTask` field, killing them recovered ONE of eight acknowledged tasks; the other seven were absent from both the recovery state and the pending queue. Election is now one critical section under a lease lock, and the state carries a monotonic epoch. A lock alone would not be enough: a worker that stalls past its TTL and is replaced can still wake up holding no lock at all, so every owned write re-reads the epoch and refuses when it no longer matches. A superseded worker stands down instead of publishing, dequeuing, re-enqueueing or deleting its successor's lease. Measured with the audit's own probes: trials now elect 1 of 8, and acknowledged tasks survive a hard kill. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: fix(memory): revalidate every schema, and report freshness per record (R02) A trusted v1 record whose source symbol had been deleted was correctly excluded from fresh recall. After the supported `migrateToV2()` the same record came back `evidence: valid`, `applicability: current`, `freshness.state: fresh` — migration laundered stale evidence into fresh advice. Two independent causes. `recallProjection` guarded live evaluation with `!isMemoryRecordVersioned`, so a migrated record kept the verdict snapshotted in its alias at migration time; the evaluator only ever needed , which every schema carries, so the guard bought nothing. And the response stamped ONE freshness object on every hit, derived from "an evaluator was bound for this pass" rather than from whether that record went through it. Evidence validity is a property of the world now, never of the schema a claim happens to be stored in. `ScoredRecord.evaluated` makes the second point structural: a record the projection skipped can no longer be advertised as freshly validated, whatever the pass as a whole did. Both regression tests fail against the original guard. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: fix(memory): apply the principal boundary to durable intakes (R03) An earlier repair gave versioned records a principal guard at the gather point. Intakes were left out: `intakeEntries()` merged every entry from every store with no principal or audience policy, and `getIntake`, `listIntakes`, `handoff` and — through `getIntake` — `checkpointIntake` all funnel through that one merge. So principal A could read principal B's `private` intake, see it in a listing, receive it in handoff, and APPEND a checkpoint to it. The guard belongs at the gather point for the same reason `acceptsRecord` does: a future intake-returning verb must inherit the boundary rather than re-derive it. Checkpoints carry no principal of their own, so one is visible exactly when its requirement is — their summaries describe the private work as directly as the requirement does. Isolation is only half the contract. A first version denied every team-shared intake too, because the entry map is last-wins and local is read second, so the surviving copy's store was the wrong thing to judge by. Team presence is now tracked separately, and the deliberate `shareIntake` promotion still reaches colleagues. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: fix(watch): let a connected reader adopt a canonical advance (R04) `refresh()` returned early whenever the dirty set was empty — which is exactly the shape of an external `crib update` that committed everything, or a clean branch switch. Consumers rebuild their read projections in `onRefresh`, and `crib serve` rebuilds the overlay FTS index there and nowhere else, so the server logged "canonical soul advanced — overlay resynced", reported the NEW head through `status`, and kept answering queries from the projection built against the OLD graph. A connected reader returned no match for a symbol a freshly started reader found immediately. A drift with nothing dirty is still a change the reader must adopt. No refresh runs — there is nothing to re-parse — so the callback carries a zero result whose only job is to say the canonical graph moved. Confirmed on an isolated copy of this repository (805 files): the connected reader now matches after an external update, saves stay at p95 2068ms. The existing drift test asserted `onDrift` fired but never that `onRefresh` did, which is why it passed throughout; the new test fails against the early return. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: fix(memory): make "remember this" actually reach recall, and ground the trust signal Reported from real use: a developer told their agent to remember a working convention, the agent called `memory_observe`, got `ok: true`, and every later `brief` and `memory_recall` returned an empty `memories` list. They concluded crib's memory does not work. Three separate defects produced that. 1. THE EVIDENCE WAS STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE, AND THE WRITE SAID OK. The payload was `[{ type: 'human-attestation', quote: '…' }]` — `type` where `kind` belongs, and a human attestation additionally needs . `observe` validated kind, subject, claim and actor and never looked at the evidence, so it staged a record that could never be activated, never recalled, and never explained. `admissibilityProblems` now decides this at write time, off the same admissibility matrix the evaluator uses so the two cannot drift. Structural admissibility is decidable the moment a claim is written, and that is the only moment its author can still fix it. 2. RECALL WAS SILENT ABOUT STAGED WORK. `memory_observe` stages an UNTRUSTED candidate and normal recall excludes untrusted claims — that gate is correct and unchanged. But recall reported the exclusion as an absence: no count, no reason, no next step. A trust gate the user cannot see is indistinguishable from a broken store. `brief` and `memory_recall` now carry a `pendingNotice` (count and next action only, never content), and the observe acknowledgement says `recallable: false` rather than implying the claim is retrievable. 3. ADMISSION DEMANDED PROOF OF SOMETHING THE CLAIM NEVER ASSERTED. Reaching local trust required `crib memory evaluate --profile <name>` to produce a gate receipt bound to HEAD and a worktree digest, then `crib memory activate`. A `convention` or `decision` admits only human-attestation and committed-policy: there is no execution to gate and no code anchor to drift. `admitAttested` is receipt-free for exactly those claims, and `crib memory remember` / `crib memory admit` make it one command. What keeps (3) from being a trust hole is that crib now MINTS the attestation instead of accepting one. `tty` was read verbatim from caller-supplied evidence, so any agent could stamp it and self-grant the trust it represents. It is now refused over MCP — an agent speaking over stdio has witnessed no terminal — and stamped by crib itself at admission, from a `process.stdin.isTTY` it checked. An agent relaying "the user told me to do X" can still propose the claim: the attestation fields are not required at STAGING, only at admission. Trust never exceeds `local`; team promotion still requires CI and a trusted ref. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: feat(onboarding): wire only the IDE in use, and ship a Python-free semantic tier TWO DEFECTS THAT MADE FIRST-RUN HOSTILE. `crib init` defaulted `--ide` to `all`, and its instruction-adapter step was hardcoded to `all` regardless — so even `crib init --ide claude` wrote GEMINI.md. A developer working in GitHub Copilot got CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, .windsurfrules, . , AGENTS.md and six MCP configs dropped into their repository, with the one file their agent reads buried among them. `copilot` was not even an accepted `--ide` value. Files nobody asked for are not a harmless default: they get committed, reviewed, and inherited by everyone who clones. `detectClients` identifies the running client from what the client itself sets, falling back to repository configuration. It deliberately ignores files crib generated: after one over-broad install every repo contains GEMINI.md, and counting that as proof of a Gemini user would make the mistake self-justifying. When nothing is identified, the vendor-neutral AGENTS.md is written and NO MCP config — a config file's location IS the client identity, and guessing one is how the spray started. `--ide all` remains, as something an operator asks for. THE SEMANTIC TIER NO LONGER NEEDS PYTHON. Reaching it required `pip install sentence-transformers` (and PyTorch) from a Node CLI, which is where installs actually died: doctor reported the degraded char-ngram fallback and the tier stayed git-checkout-only. Setup now provisions an ONNX runtime — npm packages installed into crib's embed home on demand, never into the user's project and never into crib's own dependencies, which are capped. Measured against the frozen launch gates before shipping it ( ): multilingual-e5-large scores G2 81.05% / G3 0.8814 through the ONNX path, reproducing the 81.0% / 88.1% already on record for the Python configuration. Same model, same weights, same ranking — one less toolchain. Every ladder row now carries a measured number rather than a label, including the rows that FAIL a gate: printing `small`'s real 42.5% against an 80% threshold is more honest than hiding it behind "unverified". `large` stays the default because it is the only row clearing all eight gates. `crib init` ASKS which to install and never downloads unattended; a non-interactive run says what to run instead. `--from <dir>` adopts a pre-fetched bundle for air-gapped hosts, copying rather than linking so unmounting the bundle cannot silently degrade a working tier back to lexical. Two bugs found by running it rather than reading it: the synchronous adapter deadlocked waiting for a worker `message` event while `Atomics.wait` held the event loop (readiness now travels over the same Atomics channel), and the generated worker was only written inside the install branch, so an upgraded crib kept running the previous release's worker — which hangs rather than errors when the handshake changes. Also: `crib doctor` called a working `KCRIB_EMBEDDER` override a "degraded char-ngram fallback". There is now an `external` tier that loads the provider to prove it works and says plainly that crib neither pins nor measures it. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.question: fix(embed): reconcile the two setup implementations after the rebase The rebase auto-merged ` ` without a conflict and kept BOTH `cmdEmbedSetup` implementations — the Python one from this branch and the ONNX one from mine. `tsc` caught it as a duplicate function; the package did not build. tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: feat(memory): survive an IDE session timeout, on every client Reported from real use: a Copilot or Cursor session times out and the context is gone — there is nothing to resume from. Handoff had plenty to say about intakes, checkpoints and pending captures, and every one of those requires the agent to have WRITTEN something before it stopped. An agent whose session was killed had no chance to. The lifecycle hook returned `status: checkpoint-requested`, which is a REQUEST to the agent to write a checkpoint: the design depended on precisely the thing that had just died. A timed-out session left one event saying a turn had ended, carrying no branch, no HEAD and no files — durable, and useless. Two changes, because the first alone would have helped the wrong people. 1. The lifecycle hook now records the repository anchor on every event — branch, HEAD, and the files being worked on. That is the part a hook can observe by itself, so it survives a timeout, a crash or a closed laptop with no agent cooperation at all. 2. The MCP server records the same anchor on every tool call. Of the seven client adapters exactly ONE exposes a lifecycle hook surface; Copilot, Cursor, Codex, Windsurf and Gemini are instruction-only, so a hook-based resume would have helped precisely the users who did not report the problem. Every client reaches crib through the server, which makes this the client-agnostic version of the same idea. Coalesced to one event per five minutes per distinct working set, optional at the call site, and it never throws: a resume breadcrumb is not worth a failed tool call. `handoff` surfaces it as `lastSession`, with `movedSince` set when the repository has since changed branch or HEAD — resuming against a branch you have left is worse than not resuming. It takes the newest event that HAS an anchor rather than simply the newest, so a hook predating this field degrades to older-but-useful instead of newer-but-empty, and it is absent entirely when nothing was recorded so "no hook" stays distinguishable from "no prior work". Coordinates only. Contents, prompts, transcripts and tool IO remain excluded; file NAMES were already within the capture policy that intake checkpoints use. Verified end to end against a Copilot-shaped client with no hook installed: one ordinary `query`, SIGKILL, and a new session recovers branch, HEAD and the changed file. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: fix(freshness): a busy worker is not a dead one Observed live while diagnosing this repository: `crib status` reported `workerRunning: false` for a worker that was healthily reindexing. Its heartbeat had aged past 190 seconds and returned to 1 second the moment the work finished. Revalidation runs `crib update`, whose parsing is synchronous, so a large repository blocks the event loop for as long as it takes — and a blocked event loop cannot fire the heartbeat timer. The lease therefore describes a working worker as dead, which sent an operator (me) hunting a hung process that was in fact doing their work. A live pid still holding a leased task is BUSY, and is now reported as running with `workerBusy: true`. A live pid with NO task and no heartbeat stays reported as not running: unexplained silence is not the same as visible work, and that case must remain a red flag. This does not fix the underlying property — a long synchronous revalidation still cannot beat its own heart, so a second worker starting in that window still sees a stale lease and can take the lease over. The epoch fencing added earlier makes that safe rather than corrupting (the original stands down instead of clobbering), but the takeover is spurious and wastes a full reindex. Fixing it properly means either a liveness signal that does not share the blocked thread, or an election that treats "alive and holding a task" as busy — deliberately left for its own change rather than bolted on here. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: feat(mcp): add `review` — the one call a code review needs Reported from real use: "I gave something to review, and my model read ten lines and predicted what was happening." That reads like laziness and is actually arithmetic. A reviewer needs more than the diff — who calls the changed code, and what was already decided about it — and the obvious way to get that is to read the files. Measured on this repository, reading every file a commit touched costs ~212,000 tokens. That does not fit alongside the conversation that asked for the review, so the model truncates, and truncating is what gets reported as skimming. The budget was impossible. `review` composes the answer from the graph instead: what changed, each changed DECLARATION with its signature, its code callers, and prior trusted memory about it — one bounded call, ~2,000 tokens ( ). It is NOT cheaper than a raw diff, and the docs say so. It answers what a diff structurally cannot: a diff shows changed lines, never their callers, and never the argument the team already settled. The useful pairing is diff + review, ~7k against 212k for reading files. Three defects found by running it rather than reasoning about it, each now pinned by a test: • it reported 5,156 "changed symbols" for a six-file change, because every assignment and statement in a touched file is a node. It now expands declarations only, and reports both counts so neither question is hidden. • it ranked a trivial local helper called `flag` first, because documentation sections that merely mention a word are incoming edges too. Callers are code; doc edges are excluded from the ranking and the output. • an empty caller list read as "unused". Dynamic dispatch, property access and cross-language calls all produce that same emptiness, so every such symbol now carries the label explicitly — that inference is how a reviewer talks themselves into deleting live code. Available as the `review` MCP tool and `crib review`, and named in the agent protocol every client receives, because a capability agents do not reach for is not a capability. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: fix(ui): make the memory home reachable, readable and keyboard-usable (R08) Four defects the audit measured in the memory home, each re-measured in a real browser before and after. CONTRAST 1.03:1 → 13.2:1. The lifecycle filter tabs rendered dark-theme text on the browser's default button face, i.e. effectively invisible. The cause is a template limitation worth naming: a `{{ ternary }}` inside an inline style VALUE is dropped, because the `:` of `? :` ends the CSS declaration. `background: {{ on ? a : b }}` produced no background at all and `border: 1px solid {{ … }}` lost its colour. Conditionals for those two declarations are resolved in the view model now, so the template only interpolates finished values. UNREACHABLE BELOW 900px. The Memory button carried `kc-hide-compact` and simply vanished — the same class as Tour and Blast radius, which are conveniences; memory is the product's primary surface, and the panel itself fits a 375px viewport, so the feature was unreachable rather than unusable. It now collapses to its icon. That alone was not enough: the toolbar needs 651px of controls in a 375px window, so the button existed but was laid out past the right edge. Measured, then fixed by letting the bar wrap rather than deleting controls. ESCAPE DID NOT CLOSE IT. The key handler fell through to `closePanel()` — the NODE panel — so the memory overlay could only be dismissed with the mouse. FOCUS WENT NOWHERE. Opening left focus on the toolbar button; closing left it on a button whose panel was gone. Both now managed, and the implementation is deliberately `setTimeout` rather than `requestAnimationFrame`: rAF is paused in a background tab, so an rAF version scheduled exactly one callback and silently did nothing. Focus management that only works while the tab is frontmost cannot be tested, and was not — the first two attempts here passed review and failed measurement. Also a wrong number: "Work to resume" summed `intakes.count`, which is every intake including completed and cancelled ones. `resumableCount` is now exposed separately and used, because a tile offering work to resume must not count work that is finished — that is the kind of wrong number that teaches an operator to distrust every other number on the page. NOT fixed here: pending captures and resumable intakes are still counts without per-tile actions. The panel names the next command, and the CLI performs it (`crib memory recall --include-pending`, `crib memory admit`), so this is a usability gap rather than a dead end. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: feat(onboarding): make crib mandatory everywhere and installable in one command Knowledge-crib was optional by construction. The protocol block described how to use memory; nothing said an agent had to. `crib init` wired only the client it happened to detect, so any other IDE opened the repository with no protocol at all. And the semantic tier — the difference between 2.6% and 81% paraphrase recall — prompted on a TTY and silently skipped everywhere else, so every scripted onboarding finished on the degraded lexical fallback without saying so. Three changes, in the order they matter: 1. The protocol now opens with "Knowledge-crib is MANDATORY in this repository": every agent, in every IDE, on every task; recall before planning or reading files; graph verbs before grep; no substitute store and no private side-store. It deliberately ends by saying that mandatory is not infallible — the honesty signals still govern, and an empty or `note`-qualified result is a limit of the index, never an all-clear. Stated vendor-neutrally, so the block still names no third-party tool. 2. `crib init` and `crib adapters install` default to EVERY client. This reverses a deliberate earlier fix (a Copilot user got five instruction files they had not asked for), and the reversal is the point: a client that merely failed to be detected is the one most likely to run without the rule. The narrow behaviour survives as `--ide detected` / `--client detected`, so nothing that was possible became impossible. 3. New `crib setup` — index, hooks, MCP for every client, the protocol in every instruction file, the on-device model, the memory stores, then `doctor`. The model now installs by default rather than only when a human is at a TTY; `--no-embed`, `KCRIB_NO_EMBED=1`, `--embed-model small` and `--embed-from <dir>` are the escape hatches, and the step stays last and non-fatal so a refused download degrades recall without breaking onboarding. Also: ` ` (`pnpm bootstrap`) takes a fresh checkout to a wired repo in one command, and the generated now run `crib setup` when launched inside a git work tree (`KCRIB_NO_SETUP=1` to install the binary only). Two incidental fixes found on the way: `crib init --ide claude` resolved the project root to `./claude` (`--ide` was missing from VALUE_FLAGS), and `biome check .` was already red on this branch over an `any` in a pipeline fixture — ignored now, matching the existing ` /**` precedent rather than editing what the fixture tests. Model weights are not committed: ~2.1 GB of third-party artifacts under their own licences. `crib setup` fetches and integrity-pins them on first run; every query after that is offline. Gates: 2,748 tests green across 8 packages, biome clean, onboarding:check, capabilities:check, installer:test, security:check and docs-site:check all passing. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: fix(adapters): emit the nested hook shape Claude Code actually accepts The lane-2 capture-hook writer pushed a bare {type,command} entry straight into the settings.json event bucket. Claude Code's schema nests two levels there — hooks.<Event> holds MATCHER objects, each carrying its own `hooks` array of command entries — and rejects a bare entry with "Hook matcher \"hooks\" must be an array of hook entries". The rejection is silent. No error surfaces in the session; the configured command simply never runs. So every crib-installed lifecycle hook was inert, and SessionStart never injected the `crib session bootstrap` continuation block. To the user that reads as "no memory saved for this session" — memory was intact the whole time, only the delivery was. Wrap each managed entry as {hooks:[{type,command}]}, and teach the writer to recognise the legacy flat shape as crib-owned so an existing broken settings file is repaired in place on the next install rather than gaining a duplicate beside the entry that never fired. Removal now strips crib commands out of a matcher it shares with a user hook instead of dropping the matcher whole, so uninstalling crib can never take a sibling hook with it. The existing test asserted the flat shape, which is why this shipped green; it now asserts the nested one, alongside migration and shared-matcher regressions. Also close the protocol gap the incident exposed: §2 now states that recall and handoff read different stores and that an empty recall is evidence about the claim ledger alone, never evidence that no unfinished work exists. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: feat(adapters): make crib the default at user scope, and drain the backlog automatically Crib could only ever be a per-repository choice: every client returned null for `scope: 'global'`, so instruction files and capture hooks existed solely in repositories `crib init` had been run in. Opening any other project meant an agent with no idea crib was there. Add the user-scope lane. Four clients have a user-home instruction file and now get one — Claude (~/. ), Codex (~/. ), Gemini (~/. ) and Windsurf (global_rules.md). Three honestly cannot and say so instead: Cursor has no user-home rules file at all, and Copilot's user-level instructions are a VS Code settings key rather than a file this writer owns. Claude also gains the global hook surface, so capture and the session-bootstrap continuation fire in every repository, not only wired ones. A user-level block is loaded for repositories crib has never indexed, so it carries its own applicability gate: mandatory when `.crib/` is present, explicitly ignorable when it is not. Without that, the default would tell agents to call in repos where those verbs have nothing to answer from — a memory default that manufactures failed calls. The protocol body is identical at both scopes; the gate is a prefix, not a second copy of the rules. `instructionTargets` and `settingsPath` now take the home directory from the caller, for the same reason `skillDest` already did — this module resolves home via homedir()/getpwuid, which `process.env.HOME` does not isolate, so a test that forgot to pass one would rewrite the developer's own settings. Every global-scope assertion passes an explicit temp home. Also add `crib memory activate --all` and run it from the turn-end hook, so candidates stop accumulating unread. It deliberately does NOT run a gate or invent a receipt: admission has two doors, and both require something a hook cannot fabricate — `activate` needs a receipt from a gate that really ran against this head and worktree, `admit` needs a TTY because it records that a human accepted the claim. Manufacturing either precondition is the agent self-asserting a pass, which §4 forbids. So the drain runs only when a real receipt already covers the worktree, and is a reported no-op otherwise. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.question: fix(session): degrade cleanly in repositories that have no crib index Wiring the capture hook at user scope turned an unreachable path into the common one: `crib session bootstrap` and `crib memory capture-hook` now fire in EVERY repository the user opens, and most of them have no `.crib`. tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: fix(budget): make the leak gate measure retention, and catch the leak it was built for The launch cell went red on heap growth of 58.7 MB. Two defects were behind it, and neither was the code under test. 1. The samples were never collected first. `global.gc?.()` looked like a GC, but `budget:check` runs as plain `node`, so `global.gc` was always undefined and the call was always a no-op — the comment beside it said an unavailable collector was fine because "the classifier's bound is generous enough to absorb it". It was not fine. Every sample carried uncollected garbage, so the gate measured when GC happened to run. Two consecutive CI runs of the same work reported -63 MB and +59 MB, and the passing one passed only because its number came out negative. The collector is now obtained through v8 setFlagsFromString even without the CLI flag (which the script also passes), and a run that still cannot get one is reported as DEGRADED instead of silently trusted. Measured effect on this machine: samples went from ~240 MB swinging by 63 MB to ~38 MB varying by 0.4 MB across ten cycles. 2. The rule could not detect a steady leak. It required growth to exceed ten times the FIRST-CYCLE delta — but if that delta is the leak's rate d, linear growth over N samples is exactly (N-1)*d, so with ten cycles 9d could never clear the 10d bar. A textbook 10 leak retaining 90 MB scored 90 against 100 and passed, at any rate. The tolerance is now a fixed 10x the noise floor (40 MB, unchanged in practice) plus a trend test: growth counts only when it is sustained across at least 70% of cycles. That separates the three shapes which all produce a large last-minus-first — a leak rises every cycle, a one-time retention steps once and stays flat, and GC noise rises about half the time. The failing CI series was the third. now exists. The module's docstring already claimed it did ("Pure — unit-tested over synthetic series in leak-check.test.mjs"), which is how an untested classifier ended up unable to catch its own subject. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: feat(certification): preflight certification hosts with named blockers The twenty-one native vendor cells are scheduled onto three physical machines the workflow cannot satisfy by itself. Task 10 adds the host preflight ( ) so a certification runner validates itself BEFORE any expensive work: a host missing infrastructure fails in seconds with named, actionable blockers and an uploaded report — never a five-minute run ending in "not signed in", and never a launch queued forever. Probed mechanically: native identity (WSL and GitHub-hosted runners refused by name), the launch promise's architectures, Node 22, an interactive desktop, disabled (tolerating real-host output shapes: pmset's powerd assertion annotations, ScreenSaveActive's REG_SZ data), a resolvable automation backend, and every advertised client binary with its resolved version. Attested facts a program cannot probe (dedicated accounts, signed-in clients, accessibility permission, secure storage, no unrelated projects) come from an operator attestation and are never silently satisfied. GUI execution is serialized per platform with NO job-level concurrency group — a concurrency group would cancel the queued matrix cells. Serialization is the one registered runner per platform plus a per-platform desktop lock (O_EXCL, holder named by pid) that client-desktop-certify takes before launch: a manual invocation or second runner pointed at the same desktop REFUSES to start instead of racing the active session. A fresh unparseable lock payload blocks as mid-acquisition (grace window) rather than being stolen from a live run mid-write; an uncreatable lock is a named refusal, not a crash. tasks.question: feat(memory): add `crib memory observe` — the agent write path without MCP (F16) Staging an agent observation required the `memory_observe` MCP TOOL. With the MCP server down — which, before the F18 fix, was the default state of every fresh worktree — a correct agent could record nothing at all: the only immediate-admit CLI verb is `crib memory remember`, which records that a HUMAN asserted the claim, so an agent reaching for it would mint an attestation it does not hold (and the admissibility matrix would reject it anyway, since human evidence cannot establish an implementation fact). The ledger was unreachable and the only alternative was a forged attestation. This takes exactly the route `memory_observe` takes — `api.observe` with `authorKind: 'agent'` — so the capture policy, scan, quote re-grounding and the admission gate all run identically. It is not a privileged path: - `authorKind` is hard-coded, not a flag; - a `human-attestation` evidence item is REFUSED, because the one call site allowed to present one is `crib memory remember`, which checks stdin.isTTY; - `createMemoryApi` is called WITHOUT `attestationSource` — that parameter exists to permit a tty attestation and its type only admits 'terminal'; - empty or non-array evidence is refused rather than growing the pending queue with something that can never be admitted. The ack mirrors the MCP one, including `recallable` and `nextAction`: a staged candidate reports `recallable: false`, because telling a caller "recorded" when the next recall returns nothing is true and misleading. Verified by recording this session's three learnings through it — all three admitted with `grounded: 1 exact citation(s)` and retrievable via `crib memory recall`. Along the way the gate correctly rejected a `pitfall` (needs a failing+passing receipt pair), a `convention` backed by a source-quote (needs human-attestation or committed-policy), and a quote taken from a docstring ABOVE a function rather than inside its span. tasks.author: Vishalc412
tasks.question: feat(security): refuse any non-loopback bind — local-only is a product boundary (F13) Decided 2026-09-21: knowledge-crib is permanently single-trust-domain. That turns F13 from an open gap into a stated boundary, enforced by the code instead of requested by the docs. Enforcement rather than wording, for a specific reason: isAllowedHttpCaller validates the Host header against whatever the daemon BOUND to. A `0.0.0.0` bind therefore does not merely widen the surface — it flips that check from a DNS-rebinding guard into one that APPROVES remote callers, each with the local user's full rights, since no identity, membership, revocation or per-artifact authorization exists. The control that looks like a defence becomes the thing that lets them in, and "don't do that" in a doc is the wrong instrument for a failure mode that inverts a security check. `serveHttp` now calls `assertLoopbackBind`: permits (the whole block — refusing 127.0.0.2 would be theatre, the kernel routes all of it locally), ::1, localhost, and IPv4-mapped ::ffff:127.0.0.1; throws on everything else. It THROWS rather than narrowing to loopback. An operator who asked for 0.0.0.0 wanted something this server cannot safely do, and silently binding loopback would leave them believing the exposure worked. The message names the cause, says the boundary is deliberate so nobody waits for a flag that will never come, and gives the two routes that work: an authenticating proxy in front of a loopback bind, or stdio. SECURITY.md and the capability matrix now read "out of scope, permanently — a decided product boundary" rather than "not implemented", which was true but read as an oversight. Five tests, including one pinning that the refusal explains itself rather than just refusing. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tasks.question: feat(memory): add a generated MEMORY.md digest, and surface the last session in the UI Two requests, one root cause: the ledger held the answers and nothing rendered them in a form a person could read quickly. `crib memory export [--format markdown] [--out MEMORY.md] [--include-pending]` renders a digest FROM the ledger: where I left off, unfinished work with its next safe action, what is known, what stopped holding, what is withheld. It is ONE-WAY, and that is the design rather than a shortcut. A writable memory.md would be a second source of truth — the thing the protocol forbids — and the divergence would be silent: edit the file, and every agent and IDE still reads the ledger. It is also lossy by nature, because the ledger is append-only and bi-temporal (records superseded, not edited; evidence and freshness verdicts re-derived against today's code) and markdown has nowhere to put that. The header says all of this, so a reader learns WHY editing is futile rather than being told not to. MEMORY.md is gitignored for the same reason. Withheld candidates are COUNTED, not quoted, exactly as the default recall view does — a digest printing staged claims beside admitted ones would make verified and unverified text indistinguishable, which is what the admission gate exists to prevent. `--include-pending` opts into the text under its own labelled heading. A test pins that the unadmitted text is absent by default and present with it. UI: the memory popup showed a session ID and nothing about what the session was DOING — the one question the page is opened to answer. `api.handoff` had always produced `lastSession`; `readMemoryHome` dropped it on the floor. It now flows through / and renders as a card with the progress note, /when, the changed files, and a warning when the repository has moved since. The note is the newest intake checkpoint recorded at or before the session's last activity. Checkpoints carry `recordedAt` but no session id, so authorship cannot be proven and is NOT claimed: "the note that was current when this session ended" is exactly true whichever session wrote it, and is what an operator wants. A session with no checkpoint says so rather than rendering a blank.
